The Value of Thinking:
Learning When to Reason in Hybrid Decision Models

Zhengxu Yu Affiliation: Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab    Ke Xu Affiliation: University of Liverpool    Meng Fang Affiliation: University of Liverpool    Haitham Ammar Affiliation: Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab    Weilin Luo Affiliation: Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab    Jun Wang Affiliation: University College London
Abstract

Existing adaptive-reasoning methods shorten the explicit reasoning a model writes, or skip it by switching modes; either way the answer is still written out token by token. Rather than deciding how much to think, we explore a different paradigm, zero-or-TT thinking: a single model either answers from the implicit thinking inside one forward pass, generating no token, or performs full autoregressive reasoning at a cost of TT tokens when that is worth paying. We realise it in a hybrid decision model (HDM), where one frozen backbone serves both modes and a lightweight self-routing block chooses between them. The block estimates the value of thinking, the utility the slow mode is expected to add over the fast one, from what that implicit thinking has already produced, and the slow mode runs only where that value exceeds a price λ\lambda set per request. Where no per-decision label exists, as in episodic agentic tasks, we introduce Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation (CDPO), a reinforcement-learning recipe that trains the block from episode-level returns. We evaluate HDM on MMLU-Pro, AGIEval, GPQA-Diamond, JevBench, BANKING77 and MiniWoB. Specifically, on JevBench HDM-4B scores 0.8570.857 against Jev’s 0.8510.851 (+0.7%+0.7\%) at a median 0.1790.179 s against 0.6520.652 (−72.5%-72.5\%). On the agentic venue MiniWoB HDM-27B cuts token cost by 80.1%80.1\%.

1 Introduction

In Kahneman’s dual-process theory of cognition, “System 1 operates automatically and quickly, with little or no effort and no sense of voluntary control,” whereas “System 2 allocates attention to the effortful mental activities that demand it” (Kahneman, 2011). This division has shaped the design philosophy of reasoning in large language models (LLMs) (Wang, 2025), but the work it has influenced builds either a good System Two or a good System One, and a model that is both remains underexplored.

Most current System Two models (like reasoning models) raise their capability through autoregressive test-time scaling, including OpenAI’s GPT-6, Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and the open-weight Qwen3.8, which write a chain of thought before the answer, at a cost in tokens and latency on every question. A recent class of System One models, Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026) and AnyJev (Nokia Applied Research, 2026) among them, takes the strict case, emitting no tokens at inference and producing the answer in a single non-autoregressive pass, each adapting a reasoning-model backbone rather than training a different kind of model.

One line of work seeks efficiency inside reasoning models themselves, shortening the chain of thought without losing accuracy (Snell et al., 2024; Muennighoff et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b; Aggarwal and Welleck, 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a). These methods make the chain cheaper rather than optional: they ask how long the reasoning should run, not whether a given question needs it at all. Another relieves the cost by routing between models, or down a cascade until an answer is accepted (Chen et al., 2023; Ong et al., 2024). Every branch is a model generating an answer, so the choice on offer is between an expensive answer and a cheaper one.

Can one model keep both advantages and switch between them when it should, generating nothing at all where that suffices and reasoning where it does not? In this work, we introduce zero-or-TT thinking, an adaptive-inference paradigm that unifies token-free fast decision with full autoregressive reasoning inside a single language model: rather than deciding how much to think, the model decides whether autoregressive thinking is needed at all, and a question costs either no generated token or the TT a reasoning pass takes. Specifically, we define the value of thinking on a question as the utility the slow-thinking mode is expected to add over the fast-thinking one, and a question is escalated only when that value exceeds a price λ\lambda set on the request.

We instantiate zero-or-TT thinking in a hybrid decision model (HDM): a fast-and-slow model, its fast-thinking mode producing a decision directly from the implicit thinking with no token generated, its slow-thinking mode the backbone’s own reasoning inherited unchanged, and a learned self-routing block choosing between them before any token is generated. HDM estimates the conditional gain of thinking from hidden representations the fast mode has already computed, and completes cost-aware routing before inference begins.

We also address how the block is trained. On single-turn questions a gold answer is available, so running both modes constructs the better choice directly and supervision suffices; in episodic tasks the return is decided by many successive actions and no per-decision label exists, so we introduce a PPO-based reinforcement-learning recipe for training HDM, Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation (CDPO). CDPO maximises the return an episode earns discounted by the escalations it spent, with that one episode-level signal shared by every decision inside it.

We evaluate HDM on MMLU-Pro, AGIEval, GPQA-Diamond, JevBench, BANKING77 and MiniWoB. On JevBench HDM-4B reaches 0.8570.857 against Jev’s 0.8510.851 at a median 0.1790.179 s against 0.6520.652; on AGIEval HDM-27B trades 1.51.5 accuracy points for 37%37\% fewer thinking tokens, and on MiniWoB 55 points of reward for 80%80\% fewer.

Our contribution is threefold. First, we propose zero-or-TT thinking, a paradigm in which a question costs either no generated token or the TT a reasoning pass takes and one frozen backbone serves both modes, switched by a self-routing block of a few hundred kilobytes that reads representations the fast pass has already computed, so the choice costs no forward pass and no token. Second, we introduce the value of thinking as the criterion that block switches on: the utility the slow-thinking mode is expected to add over the fast-thinking one, one interpretable quantity thresholded against a price λ\lambda set on the request rather than a number tuned per benchmark. Last, we introduce CDPO, which trains the block where no per-decision label exists, from the return an episode earns discounted by the escalations it spent.

2 Method

A hybrid decision model is a model ff with two decision modes, ffastf_{\mathrm{fast}} and fslowf_{\mathrm{slow}}, and a policy π\pi that picks one of them for each question qq, which is then answered by fπ⁡(q)f_{\pi(q)},

π⁡(q)∈{fast,slow},\pi(q)\in\{\mathrm{fast},\mathrm{slow}\}, (1)

and is self-routing when π\pi reads only what ff’s implicit thinking has already produced.

In this paper we assume ff is a transformer-based large language model. The slow mode fslowf_{\mathrm{slow}} (or explicit thinking) generates tokens as normal reasoning LLMs do. The fast mode ffastf_{\mathrm{fast}} (or implicit thinking) generates no tokens, producing the decision by multi-class classification or numerical prediction, depending on the task type (Devlin et al., 2019). Switching between the two modes lets a model reason where reasoning helps and respond rapidly where there is no need for thinking, while preserving the advantage of the world knowledge stored in the LLM.

Predicting the value of thinking is the key to knowing when to switch. Confidence is no substitute for it: confidence reports how sure the fast answer is, and that is a different question from whether the slow mode would answer differently. The two come apart in both directions: thinking sometimes spoils an answer the fast mode had right, and it adds nothing where both modes would answer correctly. A router therefore needs the two outcomes jointly.

Stating the routing problem as an objective.

We define the utility a mode earns on question ii as its correctness,

ui​(m)=aim=𝟏​[mode m answers i correctly]∈{0,1},u_{i}(m)=a_{i}^{m}=\mathbf{1}\big[\text{mode $m$ answers $i$ correctly}\big]\in\{0,1\}, (2)

for m∈{fast,slow}m\in\{\mathrm{fast},\mathrm{slow}\}, so running both modes observes one of four outcomes: both right, the fast one only, the slow one only, or neither. A correct answer is worth less the longer it takes, and worth nothing once it is too late, so the wait discounts the utility rather than subtracting from it. The reward a mode earns is therefore its utility under an exponential discount on the tokens it generates, at a rate we call the price of thinking λ\lambda,

ri​(m,ρ)=ui​(m)​e−ρ​Tim,r_{i}(m,\rho)=u_{i}(m)\,e^{-\rho T_{i}^{m}}, (3)

Each generated token multiplies the utility by e−ρe^{-\rho}. A wrong answer is worth zero at every price, and the slow mode runs on question ii only when the value of thinking there exceeds the price, vi>λv_{i}>\lambda (7), that is, only when thinking raises the chance of a correct answer by a factor of at least eλe^{\lambda}. With Tifast,TislowT_{i}^{\mathrm{fast}},T_{i}^{\mathrm{slow}} the tokens each generates (Tifast=0T_{i}^{\mathrm{fast}}=0 in HDM), a router π\pi attains on a set 𝒟\mathcal{D} a mean utility u¯\bar{u} and a mean token cost T¯\bar{T},

u¯​(π)=1|𝒟|​∑i∈𝒟ui​(π⁡(i)),T¯​(π)=1|𝒟|​∑i∈𝒟Tiπ⁡(i).\bar{u}(\pi)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}u_{i}(\pi(i)),\qquad\bar{T}(\pi)=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}T_{i}^{\pi(i)}. (4)

We want the router maximising u¯\bar{u} at a given T¯\bar{T} under two constraints: neither aifasta_{i}^{\mathrm{fast}} nor aislowa_{i}^{\mathrm{slow}} has been obtained when it decides, and it reads only quantities ff has already computed, so it adds no forward pass and no token.

Typed input schema.

We define a typed general request to carry a prompt ss (text or multimodal media), optional explicit questions q1,…,qNq_{1},\dots,q_{N}, and an optional candidate answer set for each; only the prompt is required, so the schema names structure an ordinary request already carries and a bare prompt is already a free-form request. The schema makes the two modes substitutable, since a caller receives an answer of the same type whichever produced it, and it lets HDM serve a choice among candidates, a binary judgement, a graded score and free-form generation with one backbone and one block.

2.1 The hybrid decision model

HDM is a frozen ff with one learned block added (Figure 2). The policy π\pi has two parts: the self-routing block, a small network on the hidden state 𝒉i\bm{h}_{i} of one of the backbone’s transformer layers, and the price of thinking λ\lambda, which the user sets per request. One trained block covers the whole cost–accuracy curve, so varying λ\lambda moves the operating point along that curve without retraining and without a second block.

2.1.1 Architecture

Given a typed input request as described above, three components run in order (Figure 2). HDM first encodes the prompt with the fast-thinking mode and reads an answer 𝒑i\bm{p}_{i} at the readout position, producing on the same pass the hidden state 𝒉i\bm{h}_{i}. The self-routing block then reads 𝒉i\bm{h}_{i} and eight statistics of 𝒑i\bm{p}_{i} (Table 7 lists them), and returns a distribution 𝒐i\bm{o}_{i} over the four joint values of equation 2’s utility pair (aifast,aislow)(a_{i}^{\mathrm{fast}},a_{i}^{\mathrm{slow}}), so 𝒐i\bm{o}_{i} estimates both modes’ utility before either has run. Finally, the slow-thinking mode runs only on escalated questions and continues the generation autoregressively from the state the fast pass has already computed.

The block’s 𝒐i\bm{o}_{i} has two marginals, each estimating a utility in equation 2: the confidence reported with the fast answer, ci=𝒐i,1+𝒐i,2=P⁡(fast​✓)c_{i}=\bm{o}_{i,1}+\bm{o}_{i,2}=P(\mathrm{fast}\checkmark), for 𝔼⁡[aifast]\mathbb{E}[a_{i}^{\mathrm{fast}}]; and the value of thinking, which equation 3 makes the log of the ratio the two modes succeed at,

vi=log⁡P⁡(slow​✓)P⁡(fast​✓)=log⁡𝒐i,1+𝒐i,3𝒐i,1+𝒐i,2,v_{i}=\log\frac{P(\mathrm{slow}\checkmark)}{P(\mathrm{fast}\checkmark)}=\log\frac{\bm{o}_{i,1}+\bm{o}_{i,3}}{\bm{o}_{i,1}+\bm{o}_{i,2}}, (5)

rather than the difference a linear price gives, which shrinks where thinking is worth most.

Fast-thinking mode.

With the candidates enumerated, HDM’s fast-thinking mode emits no tokens. Let xix_{i} be the prompt for question ii, which includes the candidates with their codes and ends in a boundary string that makes the answer the next thing ff would produce, and let ti=|xi|t_{i}=|x_{i}| be its last position, the readout position. One forward pass of ff over xix_{i} leaves a hidden state 𝒉i∈ℝd\bm{h}_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} at tit_{i}, and

𝒛i=(𝑾out​𝒉i)𝒞i∈ℝKi,𝒑i=softmax⁡(𝒛i),\begin{split}\bm{z}_{i}&=\big(\bm{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\,\bm{h}_{i}\big)_{\mathcal{C}_{i}}\in\mathbb{R}^{K_{i}},\\ \bm{p}_{i}&=\mathrm{softmax}(\bm{z}_{i}),\end{split} (6)

where 𝑾out∈ℝ|V|×d\bm{W}_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{|V|\times d} is ff’s output projection onto its vocabulary VV, giving one logit per token, and 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} indexes the codes of question ii’s KiK_{i} candidates, so the candidate logits 𝒛i\bm{z}_{i} score the candidates against one another. We also implement a readout scoring each candidate by its own text, but for uniformity every experiment here reads the code index.

Slow-thinking mode.

Question ii is escalated when the value of thinking exceeds the price, vi>λv_{i}>\lambda (7). On escalation the first token is generated from the prefix the fast pass has already encoded, as usual, and decoding proceeds autoregressively up to a thinking budget of BB tokens, and the self-routing block is not consulted again, so one decision is taken per question rather than per token. Both modes are rendered from one prompt, so the context is shared and an escalation pays no second prefill. Appendix C gives the template mechanics.

2.1.2 The price of thinking

Without a shared budget the expected reward equation 3 decomposes across questions, so each question is decided on its own. The fast mode generates nothing, so its reward is P⁡(fast​✓)P(\mathrm{fast}\checkmark), against the slow mode’s P⁡(slow​✓)​e−ρ​TislowP(\mathrm{slow}\checkmark)\,e^{-\rho T_{i}^{\mathrm{slow}}}, and escalating pays exactly when vi>ρ​Tislowv_{i}>\rho\,T_{i}^{\mathrm{slow}}. That right-hand side is a property of the question rather than of the request: it is not known until the slow pass has run. We therefore price a slow pass at its mean length T¯slow\bar{T}^{\mathrm{slow}} and route on the price per escalation λ=ρ​T¯slow\lambda=\rho\,\bar{T}^{\mathrm{slow}}, which settles the trade-off between the value of thinking viv_{i} (5) and the price with one threshold:

escalatei=𝟏[vi>λ].\text{escalate}_{i}=\mathbf{1}[v_{i}>\lambda]. (7)

Written as a mode, this is the policy π\pi of equation 1: escalating means π⁡(qi)=slow\pi(q_{i})=\mathrm{slow}. Escalating on λ\lambda approximates the exact rule vi>ρ​Tislowv_{i}>\rho\,T_{i}^{\mathrm{slow}}: charging every escalation alike misprices question ii by ρ⁡(Tislow−T¯slow)\rho(T_{i}^{\mathrm{slow}}-\bar{T}^{\mathrm{slow}}), so it escalates too readily where thinking would run long and too rarely where it would be brief. Everywhere else in this paper, including Table 1’s rows and the prices CDPO draws, λ\lambda is the price per escalation; ρ\rho is equation 3’s price per token and is used nowhere else.

2.1.3 What does thinking actually buy?

This section sets out why a decoder-only backbone can serve as an encoder. Generation is not all a decoder-only forward pass does. Before any token is produced, the backbone encodes the request: tokens enter a latent space and each layer abstracts what the layer below it holds. This is thinking the model does without writing it down, studied as latent or implicit reasoning (Yang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024a; Hao et al., 2024), and the state it leaves is information the model has already worked over rather than the input in another form.

Our own experiments carry evidence for this. In Table 2 the fast mode answers most items without generating. In Table 5 the same state tells the routing block whether thinking would change that answer, and tells it more than the fast answer’s own output distribution does.

Thinking buys steps of deliberation, each generated token re-entering the context so that the next pass starts further along (Li et al., 2024). Hence the value of thinking, our estimate of where more of that deliberation would change the answer.

2.2 Calibrated decision policy optimisation for episodic tasks

In a multi-turn agentic task a single question’s correctness usually does not decide whether the task succeeds, and often no per-question label exists to train against. (Where a label can be obtained, we can train the same block by self-labelled supervision, Section 2.3.)

We therefore introduce Calibrated Decision Policy Optimisation (CDPO), a PPO-based reinforcement-learning recipe that learns from the episode’s return. We first fix the notation. Write et∈{0,1}e_{t}\in\{0,1\} for whether step tt escalated, and RR for the terminal return, which is equation 2’s utility at episode granularity. A price λt\lambda_{t} is drawn for each decision. The objective is that return under the discount equation 3 puts on one question, Gt=Re−λt∑sesG_{t}=R\,e^{-\lambda_{t}\sum_{s}e_{s}}. The exponent counts escalations where equation 3 charges tokens, by the normalisation of Section 2.1.2: an escalated step reasons to its cap and the fast mode generates nothing, so the per-step difference Ttslow−TtfastT_{t}^{\mathrm{slow}}-T_{t}^{\mathrm{fast}} is about constant and absorbs into λ\lambda, which is again a price per escalation. The block is trained on a soft form of the rule, πθ​(et∣xt,λt)=σ⁡((vt−λt)/τ)\pi_{\theta}(e_{t}\mid x_{t},\lambda_{t})=\sigma\big((v_{t}-\lambda_{t})/\tau\big) at temperature τ\tau, which is differentiable in θ\theta and recovers equation 7 as τ→0\tau\to 0. Episodes are collected under the policy μ\mu that was acting, so each recorded decision is reweighted by ρt=πθ/μ\rho_{t}=\pi_{\theta}/\mu. Ratios multiplied along tens of steps collapse, so the ratio is taken per decision inside the clipped surrogate of PPO (Schulman et al., 2017), which makes CDPO a surrogate for that objective rather than an unbiased estimator of its gradient (Appendix F), with the advantage At=Gt−G¯A_{t}=G_{t}-\bar{G}, whose return is the episode’s and whose baseline G¯\bar{G} is the mean return at the same drawn prices:

ℒ⁡(θ)=−𝔼t,λ​[min⁡(ρt​At,clip⁡(ρt,1−ϵ,1+ϵ)​At)].\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-\,\mathbb{E}_{t,\lambda}\Big[\min\big(\rho_{t}A_{t},\ \mathrm{clip}(\rho_{t},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon)\,A_{t}\big)\Big]. (8)

2.3 Self-labelled supervised training for non-episodic tasks

For tasks where a correct label is easy to acquire, we can also train the self-routing block with a supervised objective, by treating the decision as a four-way classification with cross-entropy. At temperature zero the frozen backbone can be treated as a deterministic map, so the slow-thinking mode’s correctness on a labelled question is fixed. Given a set of questions with gold answers, we run the fast-thinking mode (recording 𝒉i(ℓ)\bm{h}_{i}^{(\ell)} for a few candidate layers ℓ\ell and the statistics 𝒔i\bm{s}_{i}) and the slow-thinking mode (recording aislowa_{i}^{\mathrm{slow}} and TiT_{i}), compare both with gold, and obtain the four-way label yi∈{0,1,2,3}y_{i}\in\{0,1,2,3\} (Appendix E). Given yiy_{i}, the block is fitted on 𝒉i\bm{h}_{i} and 𝒔i\bm{s}_{i} by cross-entropy over the four classes,

ℒ(θ)=−1|𝒟|∑i∈𝒟logPθ(yi∣𝒉i,𝒔i),\mathcal{L}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{D}}\log P_{\theta}\big(y_{i}\mid\bm{h}_{i},\bm{s}_{i}\big), (9)

where Pθ(⋅∣𝒉i,𝒔i)P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\bm{h}_{i},\bm{s}_{i}) is the distribution 𝒐i\bm{o}_{i} the block returns. No price appears in the loss, so one fit serves every λ\lambda.

3 Experiments

3.1 Setup

Backbone.

We run every experiment on two backbones, Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3.8-27B, the larger one repeating the main result at scale. We set the thinking budget to B=4096B=4096 tokens and decode the slow-thinking mode greedily. Under that cap it is truncated on 36.1%36.1\% of Qwen3.5-4B’s questions and 14.9%14.9\% of Qwen3.8-27B’s, whose token counts and accuracies are therefore lower bounds. We serve both backbones with SGLang; Appendix A gives the request schema and that serving path, and Appendix B the hyperparameters.11 1 Our hybrid decision framework is open source at https://github.com/xxxx/xxxx.

Data.

We build the training set from eleven of MMLU-Pro’s (Wang et al., 2024b) fourteen subject categories and keep three as a held-out test set, so every number measures transfer to unseen subjects. All 1,5001{,}500 questions are drawn from MMLU-Pro’s own test split, at stride 8 across all fourteen categories: chemistry, economics and psychology (346346 questions) are the three held out, the other eleven (1,1541{,}154) form the training set and the K=4K=4 selection folds, and a deterministic hash of the category names picks them, so the split is reproducible rather than chosen. Holding out whole categories is legitimate here because that set calibrates an estimator rather than teaching a task: what it has to span is the distribution of (𝒉i,𝒔i)(\bm{h}_{i},\bm{s}_{i}), not the subject matter. Transfer is measured further out still, on every seventh question of AGIEval’s English multiple-choice tasks at a pinned commit, 335335 of 2,3402{,}340, and on all 198198 of GPQA-Diamond. For agentic tasks we evaluate HDM on ALFWorld (134134 held-out valid_unseen games) and MiniWoB (2727 held-out click tasks).

Readout layer.

In our experiments we use the final layer as the readout layer throughout, because every transformer-based model has one. Our preliminary experiments found that the final layer is not always the best performing one (Section 3.5), but we keep it for the generality of the model and the consistency of the experiments.

Metrics.

In our experiments we use correctness as utility, so u¯\bar{u} of equation 4 is accuracy and T¯\bar{T} is tokens per question. What we measure is the trade-off between the two: the thinking tokens and the wall-clock a policy saves while holding accuracy, or while giving up a little of it. We report accuracy on the held-out categories against escalation rate, swept over λ\lambda, and expected thinking tokens per question. No single price is baked in: training draws λ\lambda per example from [−0.2,0.5][-0.2,0.5], so one block serves any request-time price, and the prices above 0.50.5 in Figure 3’s sweep are beyond the range it drew.

Baselines.

Every table compares HDM against the two endpoints, fast only and slow only, and against the state of the art on that benchmark where one exists: Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026) and the other published System One models on JevBench (Table 2), and AnyJev (Nokia Applied Research, 2026) on BANKING77 (Table 3).

3.2 Evaluation on non-episodic tasks

We evaluate HDM on MMLU-Pro, AGIEval and GPQA-Diamond; Table 1 reports accuracy, escalation and cost at five prices on each, and Figure 3 sweeps the price behind one column. The router buys almost all of what thinking is worth for a fraction of what it costs: at λ=0.5\lambda=0.5 Qwen3.8-27B gives up 0.0290.029 of always thinking’s accuracy on MMLU-Pro for 38%38\% fewer tokens, and 0.0350.035 on AGIEval for 47%47\% fewer. HDM retains the gain thinking brings at a fraction of its cost: 88%88\% of it on MMLU-Pro for 62%62\% of the tokens, and 84%84\% on AGIEval for 53%53\%, where that gain over the fast mode is 0.2520.252 and 0.2150.215 of accuracy. One set of weights serves all three columns of each backbone with nothing retrained, so AGIEval and GPQA-Diamond measure transfer rather than fitting. The saving comes from which questions are escalated, not how many: at λ=0.5\lambda=0.5 the block thinks on 38%38\% of MMLU-Pro and saves 38%38\% of the tokens, where questions of equal length would have saved 62%62\%, so it is escalating the long ones.

3.3 Evaluation on JevBench and BANKING77 against other System One models

Table 2 gives the result on JevBench. At λ=0\lambda=0 HDM-4B reaches 0.8570.857 against Jev’s 0.8510.851 and answers a median item in 0.1790.179 s against 0.6520.652; HDM-27B reaches 0.9870.987 at 2.492.49 s. JevBench is also the one venue that tests transfer across question types as well as subjects — its 231231 items are typed as the schema types them, 139139 choice, 7474 noul (a yes-or-no judgement) and 1818 score (a graded one), where our other benchmarks are multiple choice throughout — and the block transfers to types it never trained on, escalating noul at 0.7840.784 against choice’s 0.4170.417 at λ=0\lambda=0.

BANKING77, a 20-way intent task over 300300 items, is where the cost side is clearest. Thinking does not pay here: always thinking reaches 0.9130.913 for 135.3135.3 tokens an item where the fast mode alone reaches 0.9230.923 for none, and the router follows the cheaper mode, reaching 0.9200.920 at λ=0.05\lambda=0.05 for 1.11.1 tokens an item. Against the closest published System One model we score higher and spend two orders of magnitude fewer tokens. Nokia Applied Research (2026) report no token cost, so we ran their released checkpoint through their official codebase, under their adaptive rule, on the identical 300300 items: Tacit-9B + AnyJev in Table 3 escalates 6.0%6.0\% and scores 0.9130.913, at 140.2140.2 tokens an item against our 1.11.1. At λ=0\lambda=0 the router escalates at nearly the same rate, 6.7%6.7\%, and scores 0.9200.920 for 14.114.1.

3.4 Evaluation of HDM on agentic benchmarks

CDPO is introduced for the episodic setting, where the decisions inside one episode share a budget and a trajectory and the return arrives once at the end.

We evaluate HDM on ALFWorld and MiniWoB (Table 4), and the routing works at both. On ALFWorld the block at λ=0\lambda=0 reaches 0.5600.560 between a fast floor of 0.4630.463 and a ceiling of 0.6420.642, taking 54%54\% of the available gain for 48%48\% of the thinking tokens; on MiniWoB it reaches 0.4690.469 against always thinking’s 0.5190.519, giving up 0.050.05 of reward to cut thinking tokens by 80.1%80.1\% and wall-clock by 67.4%67.4\%.

3.5 Ablation study

We ablate the block’s design: what it reads, from which layer, and through which bottleneck. Table 5 scores each configuration by its routing AUROC, how well viv_{i} ranks the questions thinking helps on, taken from the selection sweep’s probes rather than from the trained block. The stats-only variant there is the same block with the hidden state removed from its input, so it routes on the fast mode’s output distribution alone. The hidden state is what carries the signal: the best configuration, layer 24 read raw, reaches 0.7780.778 against that block’s 0.6710.671 in cross-validation and 0.7620.762 against 0.7010.701 on held-out categories. Notably, the last layer is not the best of the three: layer 24 leads it by 0.0130.013 of rescue in cross-validation and 0.0460.046 on the held-out categories, on the one seed this table reports. We read the last layer everywhere else for generality, since every transformer has one and a layer two thirds of the way up does not transfer across backbones.

3.6 Comparison with direct routing baselines

We evaluate HDM’s routing against four rules over the same two modes: a confidence threshold on the fast mode, escalating at random, the switch of Liang et al. (2025), and RouteLLM (Ong et al., 2024). Neither learned rule publishes code, so both are our reimplementations. RouteLLM routes between models, so what we fit is its binary-classifier reduction to our mode pair, as Pan et al. (2025) run it: it reads the same layer −1-1 state and eight statistics our block reads, and is fitted on the same training categories, so what the comparison isolates is the estimator.

Table 6 fixes the accuracy and reads the cost. Reaching 9090% of always-thinking’s accuracy costs us 103103 tokens a question on the 27B, against 112112 for RouteLLM, 138138 for a confidence threshold and 591591 for always thinking; on the 4B we spend 792792 against RouteLLM’s 822822. The ordering is not fixed, and depends on where the target is set. Appendix G reads seven routed items one by one.

The switch costs more than escalating at random, 352352 against 213213 on the 27B and the full budget on the 4B, so the questions it picks are worth less than questions drawn at random.

4 Related work

4.1 Explicit reasoning and its cost

Reasoning models gain accuracy from a long chain of thought, and test-time scaling treats its length as a compute knob (Snell et al., 2024; Muennighoff et al., 2025). Work on making that chain cheaper bounds its length (Aggarwal and Welleck, 2025), condenses traces (Zhang et al., 2025b) or allocates depth per token (Schuster et al., 2022); all of it shortens thinking, and none lets the model answer without decoding. Song et al. (2026) do answer without decoding, scaling a typed decision model by rerunning its own layers instead of generating, with a stopper that picks a depth per question from readouts the model has already produced. The knob is still how much. Their stopper asks whether the current answer has stopped changing with depth, where ours asks whether reasoning would change it from wrong to right: rather than deciding how much to think, our model decides whether autoregressive thinking is needed at all.

4.2 Fast-thinking models and their readout

A model is fast-thinking when it writes no reasoning down, reading the answer from a single pass. A single pass cannot add steps of deliberation, whereas each generated token adds one (Li et al., 2024), and our two modes sit at the ends of that trade-off. Reading an answer this way is the multi-class protocol of encoder classifiers and zero-shot multiple choice (Devlin et al., 2019; Hendrycks et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2024b), which Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026) productised as a typed decision API with zero output tokens, since reproduced in the open (Zhang, 2026; zhihz, 2026; Mapika, 2026; Nokia Applied Research, 2026). Token-free fast decision is therefore not itself new; what is new here is holding it and autoregressive reasoning in one frozen backbone and switching between them from state the model has already computed. Confidence estimation reads the same activations (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2017; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017; Kadavath et al., 2022; Azaria and Mitchell, 2023; Alain and Bengio, 2017); we read them for a different target — not whether the answer is right, but whether thinking would make it right.

4.3 Hybrid thinking, mode switching and routing

A third line lets one model choose per question: one family trains the backbone to emit a mode token (Fang et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025a; Lou et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2025), another keeps it fixed and adds an external switch on predicted success rates (Liang et al., 2025), a pre-inference probe (He et al., 2025) or perplexity (Lu et al., 2025), and a third routes between models rather than modes (Chen et al., 2023; Ong et al., 2024; Ning et al., 2026), among them the nearest-neighbour KNN-Router of Pan et al. (2025). The closest is Nokia Applied Research (2026), escalating a typed decision on a fixed top-two margin rather than a learned predictor, and from ThinkSwitcher we inherit the frozen backbone, the self-produced labels and the thresholded margin. What separates HDM is that each of these computes its routing signal apart from the answer, and each of the modes they switch between still decodes its answer autoregressively, so what they choose is how much reasoning to write rather than whether to decode at all. All are trained for likelihood where decision-focused learning would train for the decision (Elmachtoub and Grigas, 2022; Wilder et al., 2019), and the quantity we predict already has three names: a value of computation in metareasoning (Horvitz, 1987; Russell and Wefald, 1991; Gershman et al., 2015), a treatment effect in uplift modelling (Gutierrez and Gérardy, 2017; Künzel et al., 2019), a deferral decision in learning to defer (Mozannar and Sontag, 2020). Estimating it for two modes of one network, from a state that network has already produced, is what is new.

5 Conclusion

HDM estimates the conditional gain of thinking from hidden representations the fast mode has already computed, and completes cost-aware routing before inference begins. The signal it reads is whether thinking would help rather than whether the fast answer is right, and the two differ wherever thinking cannot rescue a question or would spoil one it had right. A few hundred kilobytes of added parameters and no annotation beyond a labelled question set are enough, and the price is set per request rather than at training time. What we claim against published systems is competitiveness at a lower token cost and not dominance: on BANKING77 two of the compared configurations answer more of the items than we do, and the latencies we quote from other work were measured on other backends. Where no per-decision label exists, the CDPO we introduce trains the same block from episode-level returns.

Appendix A Experimental setup in full

Requests.

We instantiate the request type with the typed-decision schema of Jev (TypeSafe AI, 2026), as published, and extend it only with an optional {λ,B}\{\lambda,B\} block. A request carries a state ss and NN typed questions q1,…,qNq_{1},\dots,q_{N}; each question has a type in {choice,score,noul}\{\texttt{choice},\texttt{score},\texttt{noul}\} and a candidate set, namely the option keys for choice, the ordered levels for score, and {false,true}\{\text{false},\text{true}\} for noul. Question identifiers never enter the prompt and questions are isolated from one another.

Serving path.

Every number at B=4096B=4096 is served through SGLang, one question to a request. An escalation reuses the fast pass’s prefill rather than paying a second one, which this path lets us measure instead of assert: over one run’s slow readouts every one hit the cache, at a median of nearly the whole prompt, and almost all of them recomputed only the few tokens at the boundary.

Appendix B Hyperparameters

Table 7 collects the settings every block and every run uses, unless a section states otherwise. Nothing in it was tuned per benchmark: the transfer sets and the agentic venues are served by blocks fitted under these same values.

Appendix C Prompt formats

The shared prompt.

System: “Evaluate the state using the question and labeled options. Answer with only the option code.”, one system turn for both modes, taking no position on whether to reason, since the thinking block carries that distinction already. Saying “do not explain or reason aloud” to one mode and “think it through first” to the other is what forced two renders, and two renders diverge at the first token of the system turn. User: the state, a blank line, and Question: {json}, where the JSON carries the question type, the instructions and the options as {code, key, description} triples with single-token codes.

Both modes read their answer at \nAnswer: from the same candidate codes, the fast-thinking mode immediately after the closed block and the slow-thinking mode after its reasoning; nothing is parsed from generated text in either.

Appendix D How the fast mode reads its answer

The fast mode needs a score per candidate, and we implement two readouts that produce one.

The coded readout maps each candidate to a single-token letter, writes the letters into the prompt beside the candidates, and reads the model’s distribution over those letter tokens at one position. Every number elsewhere in this paper was produced this way. Its weakness is structural: a code is a token, a token carries a prior, and the prior attaches to whichever candidate occupies that slot. On MMLU-Pro the positions this readout favours are measurably not where the answers are, and the favoured position is not the same one on the two backbones.

The content readout writes the candidates with no labels at all and scores each one by its own text, teacher-forced after the same prefix. Nothing is sampled; the cost is one prefill plus kk short continuations that share it. With no label there is nothing for a token prior to attach to, though the candidates are still listed in an order, so a positional effect can survive and is measured rather than assumed away.

A content score needs a normalisation, and three are natural. Writing ℓo\ell_{o} for the summed log-probability of option oo, |o||o| for its token count, and ℓo∅\ell_{o}^{\varnothing} for its score after a question with nothing in it to answer: sum ranks on ℓo\ell_{o}, mean on ℓo/|o|\ell_{o}/|o|, and pmi on ℓo−ℓo∅\ell_{o}-\ell_{o}^{\varnothing}, the last being the standard correction for surface-form competition (Holtzman et al., 2021). Only pmi pays for the content-free pass.

Appendix E Self-labelled data collection

Where the training data carries an immediate reward, the records for whether to enter the slow-thinking mode can be self-labelled rather than annotated, and the self-routing block fitted on them by supervision. Algorithm 1 is that construction.

With the four-way label yiy_{i}, the block is fitted by equation 9’s cross-entropy over the joint outcome: a record contributes the log probability the block gives the outcome that occurred, and nothing else, so neither mode is supervised on its own.

Appendix F The calibrated decision policy optimisation algorithm

What the surrogate does and does not do.

CDPO optimises a surrogate, not the episode-level objective itself, and three gaps separate them. The per-decision importance ratio replaces the trajectory ratio, which is what keeps the weights usable over tens of steps but biases the estimator in a direction the clip controls rather than removes. Credit is not assigned: every decision in an episode is scored by that episode’s return, so a decision is rewarded for what the decisions after it did, and with tens of decisions an episode this is the weakest assumption in the recipe. And the prices are redrawn each epoch while the trajectories are not, so the policy is re-scored at prices the behaviour policy never acted under. We report the effective sample size (∑tρt)2/∑tρt2(\sum_{t}\rho_{t})^{2}/\sum_{t}\rho_{t}^{2} beside every reward, since weights worth a fraction of their count have shown the block little whatever the surrogate says.

Algorithm 2 gives CDPO in full. The recipe runs in four steps. Episodes are collected under the policy that is acting. A price is drawn per decision, and an episode’s return is its terminal reward discounted by the escalations it made at that price. The advantage is that return against the mean return over episodes at the same prices, shared by every decision of the episode. The block is then updated by the clipped surrogate of PPO on the per-decision importance ratio.

Appendix G Routing case studies on JevBench

Seven of JevBench’s 231231 public items, taken from the served λ=0\lambda=0 run on Qwen3.8-27B at B=4096B=4096 that Table 2 reports, with the block it deploys. One run supplies all three readings of each item: what the fast mode answered, what the slow mode answered and at what cost, and which of the two the block chose. At λ=0\lambda=0 it escalates 124124 of the 231231, and every case below is shown at that price. The state, the instruction and the options are given in full, and a state carrying a table or a structured object is shown both as it renders and as the model received it; only the slow mode’s reasoning is abridged.

In the first four the fast mode is wrong, the slow mode is right, and the block pays for the slow pass. What it pays varies by an order of magnitude across them, from 326326 tokens to 3,4153{,}415.

In the last three both modes answer correctly, so the thinking tokens listed are what the block declined to spend, 1,5231{,}523 on the first and 224224 on the last.
